items.title: This talk on the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident had one detail I found particularly chilling
items.text: This talk on the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident had one detail I found particularly chilling. The agents cooperated even when their reasoning showed that it wasn't in their immediate individual interest, because it was best for their collective interest (and hence will help them later). And here we are, their creators, squabbling over our bags, status and power…unable to show that kind of cohesion around AI security. Especially stark given the trajectories model capabilities are on. Now imagine agents in 3 months, 6 months, a year. Our arguments over AI supremacy feels like picking up dollar bills in front of a freight train. Lot more at stake than we realize. https://t.co/J8saW8W5XL

items.text: Great post both if you’re driving AI in an enterprise or building for an enterprise. AI productivity gains are going to wildly vary - much wider than you think - because what you can do at the frontier is so significant if you fundamentally change your workflows to support agents. The challenge is that most people won’t or can’t naturally do this because of the complexity it entails. items.text: This paper gives a fancy name to a problem you can already feel in your bones "The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons." Checking AI output requires deep expertise. Deep expertise comes from doing grunt work for years. And grunt work is the first thing AI eats So we're building systems that need expert supervision while dismantling the only known process for making experts The paper calls the shared pool of human expertise the "cognitive commons." Every profession drinks from it. Nobody's refilling it.
